subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

questions.q: A ball moves at constant speed in a horizontal circle. Which statement about the ball is correct?
options: Its K keeps changing direction, just as its velocity does.
Its K and its velocity both stay constant, as its speed does too.
Its K is constant, but its velocity changes direction.
Its K changes sign each time the ball reverses its direction.
optionWhy: A student who treats kinetic energy as a vector picks this. K is a scalar with no direction; only the velocity turns.
A student who equates constant speed with constant velocity picks this. K is constant, but the velocity changes because its direction changes.
Kinetic energy depends only on speed, K = (1/2)mv², and the speed is constant, so K is constant. Velocity is a vector, and its direction changes continuously as the ball goes around.
A student who thinks motion in a negative direction gives negative kinetic energy picks this. The velocity is squared in K = (1/2)mv², so K is positive whichever way the ball moves.
questions.explain: Kinetic energy depends only on speed, K = (1/2)mv², and the speed is constant, so K is constant. Velocity is a vector, and its direction changes continuously as the ball goes around.

questions.q: A 2.0 kg object moves in a horizontal plane with velocity components v_x = 3.0 m/s and v_y = 4.0 m/s. What is its translational kinetic energy?
optionWhy: A student who treats kinetic energy as a vector picks this: ‘components’ of 9.0 J and 16 J combined as √(9.0² + 16²). K is a scalar; the two contributions add as numbers to 25 J.

Kinetic energy depends on the speed: v² = v_x² + v_y² = (3.0 m/s)² + (4.0 m/s)² = 25 m²/s². K = (1/2)mv² = (1/2)(2.0 kg)(25 m²/s²) = 25 J. Equivalently, (1/2)m v_x² + (1/2)m v_y² = 9.0 J + 16 J, added as numbers, because K is a scalar.
A student who adds the velocity components to get the speed picks this: v = 3.0 + 4.0 = 7.0 m/s. The components are perpendicular, so v = √(3.0² + 4.0²) = 5.0 m/s.
A student who leaves out the factor 1/2 picks this: mv² = (2.0 kg)(25 m²/s²). K = (1/2)mv².
questions.explain: Kinetic energy depends on the speed: v² = v_x² + v_y² = (3.0 m/s)² + (4.0 m/s)² = 25 m²/s². K = (1/2)mv² = (1/2)(2.0 kg)(25 m²/s²) = 25 J. Equivalently, (1/2)m v_x² + (1/2)m v_y² = 9.0 J + 16 J, added as numbers, because K is a scalar.

questions.q: A cart has a translational kinetic energy of 12 J. Cargo is then removed so that the cart’s total mass is halved, and the cart moves at twice its original speed. What is the cart’s new translational kinetic energy?
optionWhy: A student who takes K as proportional to v rather than v² picks this: (1/2)(2) = 1, so K is unchanged. The speed is squared, so doubling it alone makes K four times as large.
A student who thinks mass does not affect kinetic energy picks this, applying only the speed factor of 4. K is proportional to m, so halving the mass halves K.
A student who applies the mass factor the wrong way round picks this: 4 × 2 = 8, as if halving the mass doubled K. K ∝ m, so halving m multiplies K by 1/2.
K = (1/2)mv². Halving m multiplies K by 1/2; doubling v multiplies it by 2² = 4. The new K is (1/2)(4)(12 J) = 24 J.
questions.explain: K = (1/2)mv². Halving m multiplies K by 1/2; doubling v multiplies it by 2² = 4. The new K is (1/2)(4)(12 J) = 24 J.
questions.working: K₂/K₁ = (m₂/m₁)(v₂/v₁)² = (1/2)(2)² = 2 ⇒ 24 J. Distractors: K ∝ mv ⇒ (1/2)(2) = 1 ⇒ 12 J; mass ignored ⇒ 4 ⇒ 48 J; mass factor inverted ⇒ 2 × 4 = 8 ⇒ 96 J.

questions.q: A train moves along a straight, level track. The figure shows a ball rolling along the train’s floor, opposite to the train’s motion, with the speeds and the ball’s mass labeled. Treat the ball as a particle. What is the ball’s translational kinetic energy measured by an observer at rest on the ground?
optionWhy: A student who adds the two speeds whatever their directions picks this: (1/2)(0.40)(24 m/s)². The ball moves backward relative to the train, so its speed relative to the ground is 20 − 4.0 = 16 m/s.

A student who thinks every observer measures the same kinetic energy picks this, using the speed relative to the train: (1/2)(0.40)(4.0)² = 3.2 J. That is the value for an observer on the train; relative to the ground the ball moves at 16 m/s.
Relative to the ground, the velocities add as vectors: taking the train’s direction as positive, v = +20 m/s − 4.0 m/s = +16 m/s. K = (1/2)mv² = (1/2)(0.40 kg)(16 m/s)² = 51 J.
A student who adds kinetic energies from the two frames picks this: (1/2)(0.40)(20)² + (1/2)(0.40)(4.0)² = 80 J + 3.2 J. Velocities add between frames; kinetic energies do not, because of the square.
questions.explain: Relative to the ground, the velocities add as vectors: taking the train’s direction as positive, v = +20 m/s − 4.0 m/s = +16 m/s. K = (1/2)mv² = (1/2)(0.40 kg)(16 m/s)² = 51 J.

questions.q: Which of the following describes the work done on a system by a force exerted on it?
options: Energy transferred into or out of the system by the force as the system moves.
The force exerted on the system multiplied by the time for which it is exerted.
Energy that the force puts inside the system, which the system then contains as work.
The effort needed to exert the force, whether or not the system ever moves at all.
optionWhy: Work is a transfer of energy between a system and its surroundings by a force, and it happens only while the point where the force is exerted moves with a component along the force. Positive work transfers energy in; negative work transfers it out.

A student who thinks work depends on how long a force is exerted picks this. Work is the force component along the displacement times the displacement; time does not appear, and a force on an object that does not move does no work however long it is exerted.

A student who thinks of work as something a system holds picks this. Work is energy in transit; the energy transferred shows up as a form of the system’s energy, such as kinetic energy, not as stored ‘work’.
A student who uses the everyday meaning of work as effort picks this. A force on a system that does not move transfers no energy to it, however tiring the force is to exert.
questions.explain: Work is a transfer of energy between a system and its surroundings by a force, and it happens only while the point where the force is exerted moves with a component along the force. Positive work transfers energy in; negative work transfers it out.

questions.q: Identical blocks are released from rest at the tops of the three frictionless ramps shown and slide to the floor. Which claim correctly compares the work done by gravity on the blocks, from the top of each ramp to the floor?
options: It is greatest on Ramp 3, the longest.
It is greatest on Ramp 1, the steepest.
It is the same on all three ramps.
It is zero: gravity is conservative.
optionWhy: A student who thinks gravity’s work grows with the distance traveled picks this. On a longer ramp the component of gravity along the ramp is smaller, mg sin θ, and over the length h/sin θ it does the same work, mgh.
A student who compares forces instead of work picks this. The component of gravity along Ramp 1 is the largest, but it acts over the shortest distance; the product is mgh on every ramp.

Gravity is a conservative force, so the work it does depends only on the initial and final positions: W_g = mgh for each block, because each drops the same height h. The ramp’s length and steepness change how the work is spread along the path, not its total.
A student who thinks a conservative force does no work picks this. Gravity does positive work mgh on each block as it descends; ‘conservative’ means only that this work does not depend on the path.
questions.explain: Gravity is a conservative force, so the work it does depends only on the initial and final positions: W_g = mgh for each block, because each drops the same height h. The ramp’s length and steepness change how the work is spread along the path, not its total.
questions.working: W_g = (mg sin θ)(L) along a ramp of angle θ and length L = h/sin θ, so W_g = mgh on every ramp. Distractors: longest ramp (Ramp 3) from W = mgL; steepest ramp (Ramp 1) from the largest force component; zero from ‘conservative means no work’.

questions.q: A block attached to a spring slides back and forth along a rough incline. Which of the forces exerted on the block is nonconservative, and why?
options: Kinetic friction: it destroys some of the block’s energy, so energy is not conserved.
Gravity: it changes the block’s kinetic energy, so it does not conserve its energy.
The spring force: it does negative work on the block while the block compresses the spring.
Kinetic friction: its work on the block depends on the length of the path the block takes.
optionWhy: A student who thinks nonconservative forces destroy energy picks this. Friction is nonconservative, but energy is conserved: friction transfers mechanical energy into thermal energy. The defining property is the path dependence of its work.

A student who thinks a conservative force does no work on an object picks this. Gravity does change the block’s kinetic energy, but its work depends only on the change in height, so it is conservative.

A student who thinks a force that does negative work is nonconservative picks this. The spring force does negative work during compression and positive work during extension; its work depends only on the initial and final stretch, so it is conservative.

Kinetic friction always opposes the block’s motion relative to the incline, so its work is −F_f times the path length and depends on the path; it is nonconservative. Gravity and the spring force do work that depends only on the block’s initial and final positions.
questions.explain: Kinetic friction always opposes the block’s motion relative to the incline, so its work is −F_f times the path length and depends on the path; it is nonconservative. Gravity and the spring force do work that depends only on the block’s initial and final positions.

questions.q: A ball tied to a string moves at constant speed in a horizontal circle on a frictionless table. Which claim about the work done on the ball by the tension T in the string during one quarter of a revolution is correct?
options: It is zero, as the tension is perpendicular to the ball’s velocity at each instant.
It is positive, because the string pulls on the ball all the time that it moves.
It is T times the straight-line distance between the start and end of the quarter turn.
It is a vector pointing to the circle’s center, the way the tension points.
optionWhy: The tension always points toward the center of the circle, and the velocity is always tangent to it, so the angle between the tension and each small displacement is 90° and T⃗ · dr⃗ = 0 throughout. The tension changes the direction of the ball’s motion but not its speed or kinetic energy.
A student who thinks every force on a moving object does work picks this. A force does work only through its component along the motion; the tension has no such component at any point.
A student who multiplies the full force by the size of the displacement, ignoring their directions, picks this. At every instant the tension is at 90° to the ball’s motion, so it does no work.
A student who treats work as a vector picks this. Work is a scalar, the dot product of force and displacement, and here it is zero.
questions.explain: The tension always points toward the center of the circle, and the velocity is always tangent to it, so the angle between the tension and each small displacement is 90° and T⃗ · dr⃗ = 0 throughout. The tension changes the direction of the ball’s motion but not its speed or kinetic energy.

questions.q: A ball is held at rest above the floor of a room. A student says that the ball “has gravitational potential energy.” Which statement correctly describes this gravitational potential energy?
options: It belongs to the ball alone, because the ball has mass and is held high above the floor.
It belongs to the ball–floor system, because the height is measured up from the floor.
It belongs to the ball–Earth system and depends on how far apart the ball and Earth are.
It belongs to the ball–Earth system and is directed downward, the way Earth pulls.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a single object can have potential energy of its own picks this. Potential energy needs two or more interacting objects: the ball’s gravitational potential energy is shared with Earth, which exerts the gravitational force on it.

A student who mistakes the reference level for the interacting partner picks this. The floor only marks where U_g = 0 is chosen; the gravitational interaction, and so the potential energy, is between the ball and Earth.

The gravitational force is a conservative interaction between the ball and Earth, so the potential energy belongs to the ball–Earth system, a system of two interacting objects. Its value depends on their relative positions, here the height of the ball above Earth’s surface. The ball on its own has no potential energy.
A student who treats potential energy as a vector picks this. The system is right, but potential energy is a scalar: it has a value, which may be positive or negative, and no direction.
questions.explain: The gravitational force is a conservative interaction between the ball and Earth, so the potential energy belongs to the ball–Earth system, a system of two interacting objects. Its value depends on their relative positions, here the height of the ball above Earth’s surface. The ball on its own has no potential energy.

questions.q: A satellite moves in a circular orbit around Earth. Which statement about the gravitational potential energy of the Earth–satellite system is correct?
options: It has the same value at every point of the orbit, as the separation never changes.
It changes direction around the orbit, as it points from the satellite toward Earth.
It is zero all the way around, since a weightless satellite feels no gravitational pull.
It is undefined, since the satellite is not at a height above any ground to measure from.
optionWhy: Potential energy is a scalar associated with the positions of the objects in the system. U_g = −Gm_1m_2/r depends only on the separation r of Earth’s center and the satellite, which is constant in a circular orbit, so U_g has the same value all the way around.
A student who treats potential energy as a vector picks this. The gravitational force on the satellite changes direction around the orbit, but potential energy is a scalar and has no direction.

A student who thinks gravity does not act on objects in orbit picks this. Earth’s gravitational force is what keeps the satellite in orbit; the system has U_g = −Gm_1m_2/r, which is negative, not zero, with the usual zero at infinite separation.

A student who thinks potential energy means height above the ground picks this. Gravitational potential energy depends on the separation of the interacting objects; U_g = −Gm_1m_2/r applies at any separation, with no ground needed.
questions.explain: Potential energy is a scalar associated with the positions of the objects in the system. U_g = −Gm_1m_2/r depends only on the separation r of Earth’s center and the satellite, which is constant in a circular orbit, so U_g has the same value all the way around.

questions.q: An object in a system is at a position of stable equilibrium. The object is moved a small distance in the +x direction and released from rest. Which statement describes what happens immediately after the object is released?
options: No force acts on the object at that instant, because its velocity is zero then.
A force in the +x direction accelerates the object farther from the equilibrium position.
A force in the −x direction accelerates the object back to the equilibrium position.
The object stays at rest where it is released, because its equilibrium position is stable.
optionWhy: A student who thinks zero velocity means zero force picks this. The force depends on the object’s position: away from equilibrium it is not zero, even at the instant the object is at rest.

A student who has the stable and unstable cases the wrong way round picks this. A force in the direction of the displacement is the mark of an unstable equilibrium; at a stable one the force points back toward equilibrium.

At a stable equilibrium position, a small displacement results in a force opposite to the displacement. The object was displaced in the +x direction, so the force is in the −x direction and accelerates it back toward the equilibrium position.

A student who takes ‘stable’ in its everyday sense of ‘not moving’ picks this. Stable means that the force after a small displacement points back toward equilibrium, so the released object accelerates back.
questions.explain: At a stable equilibrium position, a small displacement results in a force opposite to the displacement. The object was displaced in the +x direction, so the force is in the −x direction and accelerates it back toward the equilibrium position.

questions.q: A ball is thrown straight upward. Air resistance is negligible. A student chooses the ball alone as the system. Which statement correctly describes the energy of this system while the ball is rising?
options: Its kinetic energy is gradually converted into gravitational potential energy of the ball.
Its kinetic energy decreases as Earth’s gravitational force does negative work on it.
Its total energy stays constant, since energy is conserved in every interaction.
Its kinetic energy decreases as the upward force from the throw is used up.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a single object has its own gravitational potential energy picks this. U_g belongs to the ball–Earth system; with the ball alone as the system there is no U_g to convert into, and the decrease in K is energy transferred out by gravity's work.

A system of the ball alone can have only kinetic energy. Earth is outside the system, so its gravitational force is external; it points opposite to the ball's upward displacement, does negative work, and transfers energy out of the system, so K decreases.

A student who thinks conservation of energy makes every system's energy constant picks this. Energy is conserved overall, but this system's energy decreases: Earth, outside it, does negative work on the ball.

A student who thinks the ball carries a force from the throw picks this. Once the ball leaves the hand, no upward force acts on it; the only force is gravity, and it is gravity's negative work that reduces K.
questions.explain: A system of the ball alone can have only kinetic energy. Earth is outside the system, so its gravitational force is external; it points opposite to the ball's upward displacement, does negative work, and transfers energy out of the system, so K decreases.

questions.q: Which of the following systems can have potential energy?
options: A block and the ideal spring that it is compressing
A single rock on its own, held at rest high above the ground
A crate and the rough floor across which the crate slides
A lump of clay on its own, squashed flat by a blow
optionWhy: An ideal spring changes shape reversibly and pushes back on the block with a conservative force, so the block–spring system has elastic potential energy, U_s = (1/2)k(Δx)², as well as kinetic energy.
A student who thinks an object on its own has gravitational potential energy picks this. U_g belongs to the rock–Earth system; a system of the rock alone has only kinetic energy, here zero.

A student who thinks friction stores energy as potential energy picks this. Friction is nonconservative: the energy it removes becomes thermal energy and sound, and no potential energy is associated with it.

A student who thinks any change of shape stores potential energy picks this. Clay does not spring back; its deformation is permanent, so the energy of the blow is dissipated as thermal energy and sound, not stored.
questions.explain: An ideal spring changes shape reversibly and pushes back on the block with a conservative force, so the block–spring system has elastic potential energy, U_s = (1/2)k(Δx)², as well as kinetic energy.

questions.q: A sled slides across level snow and comes to rest. Which statement about the sled's kinetic energy is correct?
options: It was used up by friction, so that it no longer exists anywhere at all.
It was turned into the friction force that brought the sled to a stop.
It became thermal energy of the sled, the snow and the air, and some sound.
It was stored as potential energy of the system made up of the sled and the snow.
optionWhy: A student who thinks energy is used up picks this. Energy is never destroyed: the kinetic energy is still there as thermal energy and sound, even though it is spread out and hard to notice.

A student who treats force and energy as the same kind of thing picks this. Friction is a force (in newtons) exerted by the snow while the sled slides; it transferred the energy by doing negative work but is not itself energy.

Energy is conserved in all interactions. Kinetic friction and air resistance are nonconservative, so they dissipate the sled's kinetic energy as thermal energy of the surfaces and the air, and as sound; the total energy is unchanged.
A student who thinks friction stores energy as potential energy picks this. Friction is nonconservative, so no potential energy is associated with it; the energy cannot come back as kinetic energy.
questions.explain: Energy is conserved in all interactions. Kinetic friction and air resistance are nonconservative, so they dissipate the sled's kinetic energy as thermal energy of the surfaces and the air, and as sound; the total energy is unchanged.

questions.q: Students X and Y each lift an identical box from the floor to the same shelf. Each box starts and ends at rest. X takes 2 s and Y takes 4 s. Which statement is correct?
options: X transfers more energy to the box–Earth system, because X lifts it faster.
X transfers the same energy as Y at twice Y’s rate, because X takes half the time.
Y transfers more energy to the box–Earth system, because Y pushes for longer.
X and Y deliver the same power, because they do the same amount of work.
optionWhy: A student who thinks doing a task faster takes more energy picks this. Both boxes rise the same height and end at rest, so both systems gain mgΔy; X transfers it at a greater rate, not in a greater amount.
Each box–Earth system gains the same energy, mgΔy (the box starts and ends at rest, so ΔK = 0). X transfers it in half the time, so X's average power, ΔE/Δt, is twice Y's.
A student who thinks the energy a force transfers depends on how long it acts picks this. Work depends on force and displacement; both systems gain the same mgΔy.
A student who treats power as the same thing as work picks this. Power is work divided by time: with the same work, X, taking half the time, delivers twice the average power.
questions.explain: Each box–Earth system gains the same energy, mgΔy (the box starts and ends at rest, so ΔK = 0). X transfers it in half the time, so X's average power, ΔE/Δt, is twice Y's.

questions.q: A ball is released from rest and falls. Air resistance is negligible. Consider the ball–Earth system while the ball falls. Which statement about power for this system is correct?
options: U_g is converted into K at a rate that increases steadily as the ball speeds up.
No power is involved, since no energy enters or leaves the ball–Earth system.
U_g is converted into K at a constant rate, since the gravitational force is constant.
U_g is converted into K at a rate that decreases as the value of U_g becomes smaller.
optionWhy: Power includes conversion within a system. The rate at which U_g becomes K is dK/dt = F_g v = mgv, and v increases steadily during free fall, so the rate increases.
A student who thinks power describes only transfers across a system's boundary picks this. Power is also the rate of conversion within a system; here U_g turns into K at the rate mgv.
A student who thinks power depends only on the force picks this. The rate is F_g v = mgv; the force is constant but the speed increases, so the rate increases.
A student who links a rate to the amount remaining picks this. The rate of change of U_g is −mgv, whose size grows as the ball speeds up, whatever the value of U_g.
questions.explain: Power includes conversion within a system. The rate at which U_g becomes K is dK/dt = F_g v = mgv, and v increases steadily during free fall, so the rate increases.

questions.q: A 60 kg sprinter starts from rest and reaches a speed of 8.0 m/s in 2.5 s along a level track. What is the average rate at which the sprinter's kinetic energy increases during the 2.5 s?
optionWhy: A student who treats kinetic energy as proportional to speed picks this: (1/2)(60)(8.0) = 240, divided by 2.5 s. K = (1/2)mv² uses the square of the speed.
A student who writes the kinetic energy as mv² picks this: 60 × 64 = 3840 J, divided by 2.5 s. With K = (1/2)mv², ΔK = 1920 J.
ΔK = (1/2)(60)(8.0)² = 1920 J, gained in 2.5 s, so the average power is ΔK/Δt = 1920/2.5 = 768 W ≈ 7.7 × 10² W.
A student who multiplies the energy by the time picks this: 1920 J × 2.5 s. Power is energy per unit time, so the energy is divided by the time.
questions.explain: ΔK = (1/2)(60)(8.0)² = 1920 J, gained in 2.5 s, so the average power is ΔK/Δt = 1920/2.5 = 768 W ≈ 7.7 × 10² W.

questions.q: A small satellite orbits a planet whose mass is about 10²⁰ times the satellite's mass. In analyzing the orbit, the planet is treated as stationary. Which statement correctly justifies this?
options: Each exerts an equal force on the other, but the planet's acceleration is tiny.
The planet pulls on the satellite much harder than the satellite pulls on it.
The satellite's mass is far too small for it to exert a gravitational force at all.
In orbit the satellite is weightless, so the two of them exert no forces on each other.
optionWhy: The gravitational forces the satellite and planet exert on each other are a Newton's third-law pair, equal in magnitude. By Newton's second law the planet's acceleration is that force divided by its mass, about 10²⁰ times smaller than the satellite's, so its motion is negligible.
A student who thinks the more massive object exerts the larger force picks this. The two forces are a third-law pair and have equal magnitudes; the difference is in the accelerations they produce.
A student who thinks only massive bodies exert gravitational forces picks this. The satellite pulls on the planet with a force equal in magnitude to the planet's pull on it, G Mm/r².

A student who thinks there is no gravity in orbit picks this. Gravity is the force that keeps the satellite in orbit; the satellite is only apparently weightless, because gravity is the only force on it.
questions.explain: The gravitational forces the satellite and planet exert on each other are a Newton's third-law pair, equal in magnitude. By Newton's second law the planet's acceleration is that force divided by its mass, about 10²⁰ times smaller than the satellite's, so its motion is negligible.

questions.q: The diagram shows a satellite's elliptical orbit around a planet, with two points of the orbit marked P and A. The only force on the satellite is the planet's gravity. Which quantity is greater when the satellite is at P than when it is at A?
options: the system's total mechanical energy
the satellite's angular momentum
the system's potential energy U_g
the kinetic energy of the satellite
optionWhy: A student who equates the system's total energy with the satellite's kinetic energy picks this. With only gravitational forces between the two objects, the total mechanical energy is the same at P and A; the larger K at P is balanced by a lower U_g.

A student who thinks angular momentum increases with speed picks this. The satellite's angular momentum about the planet is constant; at P its larger speed is matched by its smaller distance, so rv is the same at P and A.
A student who compares the sizes of the negative values picks this, since |U_g| is larger at P. U_g = −GMm/r is more negative, so smaller, at P; it is greater at A, farther from the planet.

P is much closer to the planet than A. The system's mechanical energy is constant, and U_g = −GMm/r is lower (more negative) at P, so K is greater at P: the satellite moves fastest at its closest point.

questions.q: A satellite is at distance r from the center of a planet of radius R. The gravitational potential energy U of the satellite–planet system is defined to be zero when r is infinite. Which graph shows U as a function of r for r ≥ R?
options: Graph 1
Graph 2
Graph 3
Graph 4
optionWhy: A student who writes the potential energy as +GMm/r picks the positive curve falling toward zero. With zero at infinity, U = −GMm/r is negative at every finite distance.

A student who uses U = mgΔy at every distance picks the straight line rising from zero at the surface. That treats the field as constant and puts the zero at the surface; for a satellite system U = −GMm/r, which levels off toward zero.
U = −GMm/r is negative for every finite r, has its lowest value, −GMm/R, at the surface, and rises toward zero as r increases, more and more slowly because its slope GMm/r² decreases.

A student who keeps the zero of potential energy at the planet's surface picks the curve rising from zero at R. That curve, GMm(1/R − 1/r), has the right shape but the wrong zero: the stem defines U = 0 at infinite separation.
questions.explain: U = −GMm/r is negative for every finite r, has its lowest value, −GMm/R, at the surface, and rises toward zero as r increases, more and more slowly because its slope GMm/r² decreases.
questions.working: U = −GMm/r: negative at every finite r, equal to −GMm/R at the surface, and increasing toward zero (from below) as r increases, with slope GMm/r² that decreases with r.

figure.alt: Four graphs, numbered 1 to 4, each of U (vertical axis, positive upward, with the r axis across the middle) against r (horizontal axis), with R marked on the r axis; each curve is drawn for r ≥ R. Panel 1: the curve starts at a positive value at R and falls, ever less steeply, toward zero, staying above the r axis. Panel 2: a straight line that starts at zero at R and rises steadily. Panel 3: the curve starts at a negative value at R and rises, ever less steeply, toward zero, staying below the r axis. Panel 4: the curve starts at zero at R and rises, ever less steeply, toward a positive value.
